strengths: Addresses an important and clearly motivated problem — extrapolation of dynamic 3D scenes beyond the training time window — which most time-conditioned deformation methods do not handle

Strong and consistent quantitative gains on two standard benchmarks (D-NeRF and NVFI), with improvements of ~3-4 dB PSNR on D-NeRF and up to ~10 dB on NVFI over competitive baselines including GaussianPrediction and Deformable-GS

The core idea — decoupling interpolation from extrapolation by training an autoregressive Transformer Latent ODE on frozen Gaussian trajectories, avoiding explicit timestamp conditioning — is sensible and well-motivated for temporal generalization
The dynamic sequence separation strategy (querying the frozen interpolation model to build diverse input/suffix training pairs) is a clever way to generate supervision for forecasting
Both a variational and deterministic variant are reported, providing some insight into the modeling choice, and the second-derivative smoothness regularizer is simple and reasonable
Paper is generally well-written with a clear two-stage formulation and adequate implementation detail (architecture sizes, solver, hyperparameters)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a composition of existing components — Deformable 3DGS (Stage 1), Latent ODE/VDODE from Rubanova et al. [32], and a Transformer encoder — applied to Gaussian parameter trajectories; the main new elements are the two-stage decoupling and a simple finite-difference smoothness penalty

No ablation studies. The contribution of the second-derivative regularizer, the KL annealing, the curriculum learning strategy, the choice of latent dimension, and the variational vs. deterministic design are never isolated. Given that the method consists of many moving parts, ablations are essential to substantiate the design claims
A broken cross-reference ('Section ??' in Section 4.1.2) leaves the curriculum learning procedure undescribed, hurting completeness and reproducibility

Stage 2 supervision is entirely self-generated from the frozen Stage-1 model (pseudo ground truth). There is no analysis of error compounding or of how sensitive the system is to Stage-1 quality; the extrapolation model may simply be learning to imitate the deformation MLP's inductive bias rather than true scene dynamics

The abstract's claim of 'halving perceptual error relative to the strongest baselines' does not hold on D-NeRF (LPIPS 0.0504 vs. 0.0529 for Deformable-GS); claims are stronger than the evidence on one of the two datasets

Evaluation is thin on qualitative evidence: only a single qualitative comparison on one scene (Mutant); no user study, no visualization of predicted trajectories/uncertainty despite the variational formulation, and no analysis of long-horizon degradation
Several scenes (Standup, Trex, Bouncingballs) show performance comparable to or below baselines, but these cases are not analyzed; the failure modes of the approach are not discussed
No computational cost, training time, or runtime analysis despite the emphasis on real-time rendering; no code release or supplementary material mentioned, limiting reproducibility

It is unclear whether the claimed 'optional rendering losses' are used in the reported results, and whether baselines were retrained or tuned under the identical 80/20 and 75/25 temporal splits — protocol fairness cannot be verified from the text

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: temporal extrapolation (true forecasting) of dynamic 3D scenes, as opposed to the interpolation setting that most 3DGS/NerF dynamic methods target. The motivation and problem framing are clear.
The two-stage design (learn a frozen interpolation oracle, then train a trajectory-conditioned extrapolator) is sensible and avoids time-conditioned deformation fields that fail out-of-distribution.
Both a deterministic and a variational Latent ODE variant are reported, and the second-derivative smoothness regularizer is a reasonable, lightweight addition.
Quantitative gains over existing baselines (TiNeuVox, 4D-GS, Deformable-GS, GaussianPrediction) on D-NeRF and NVFI are large in the reported tables, and qualitative residual maps are provided.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the method is essentially a direct application of the Latent ODE of Rubanova et al. [32] to per-Gaussian parameter sequences on top of an off-the-shelf Deformable 3DGS stage. All core components (canonical + deformation MLP, Transformer encoder, Latent ODE, ELBO training) are adopted from prior work; the combination itself is the main contribution, which is incremental for a top-tier venue.

Questionable supervision setup: Stage 2 is trained exclusively on trajectories generated by the frozen Stage 1 interpolation model, i.e., the 'ground-truth suffixes' are synthetic outputs of D_ω queried within the training window, never real future observations. The paper does not analyze or justify why a model trained purely on self-distilled, in-window trajectories can predict truly unseen future dynamics, and this is the crux of the central claim. This also risks simply distilling any artifacts of the interpolation model.

Incomplete evaluation: (1) no ablation studies — the contributions of the ODE formulation itself (vs. a plain Transformer/MLP autoregressive forecaster), the smoothness regularizer, the curriculum, and the variational inference are never isolated; (2) no analysis of performance as a function of extrapolation horizon; (3) evaluation is limited to two mostly synthetic/controlled datasets, with no real-world video benchmarks; (4) it is unclear how baselines were adapted for the extrapolation task and whether their extrapolation protocols are comparable.

The headline claims (up to 10 dB PSNR improvement, halved LPIPS) are unusually large and deserve more scrutiny: with no future-frame supervision and no ablations, such margins raise concerns about evaluation protocol, test-time information leakage, or unfavorable baseline configurations. Details of the test split and how many unseen frames are evaluated are thin.

Presentation and rigor issues: a broken reference ('Section ??') remains in Section 4.1.2, the caption of Figure 2 and the text ('shown by 2') are sloppy, only one qualitative example (Mutant) is shown, and no supplementary material, code release, or reproducibility statement is mentioned. Given a 12-page paper, the experiments section is comparatively thin.

Per-Gaussian independent forecasting: the Latent ODE operates on each Gaussian's trajectory separately, so inter-Gaussian coupling and scene-level consistency of long-horizon rollouts (e.g., drifting or diverging Gaussians) is not analyzed; there is no discussion of failure modes or of non-periodic/non-recurring dynamics, despite the method's feasibility argument resting on recurring motion.

Missing related baselines: no comparison to simpler sequence models (e.g., per-Gaussian linear/quadratic extrapolation, spline fitting, or an LSTM forecaster), which would be essential to establish that the ODE machinery is actually responsible for the gains rather than the trajectory-based training scheme.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper correctly identifies that time-conditioned dynamic rendering methods interpolate well but fail at temporal extrapolation, and positions the work against this gap.

The two-stage design is sensible: a frozen high-fidelity interpolation model is used as a trajectory oracle to generate diverse pseudo-sequential training data (dynamic sequence separation), which addresses data scarcity for forecasting without extra captures.

Strong empirical results on two standard benchmarks (D-NeRF and NVFI), with consistent improvements over relevant baselines including GaussianPrediction, Deformable-GS, 4D-GS, and TiNeuVox; gains of 3-4 dB PSNR on D-NeRF and up to ~10 dB on NVFI with substantially lower LPIPS.

Both a variational and deterministic variant are presented and evaluated, giving insight into whether stochasticity modeling matters, and the variational ODE formulation is technically sound (reparameterization, ELBO with annealed KL).
The autoregressive, time-index-free formulation (conditioning on past trajectories rather than absolute timestamps) is a principled way to avoid out-of-distribution time inputs.
weaknesses: Limited ablation support for the claimed contributions. The second-derivative smoothness regularizer is presented as a key novelty, but there is no ablation isolating its effect, nor any ablation of the curriculum learning strategy, Transformer encoder vs. alternatives, or the ODE itself vs. a direct sequence-to-sequence decoder. Only the Var-vs-Det comparison is provided.

Novelty is primarily compositional: Transformer-based Latent ODEs (Rubanova et al.) and deformable 3DGS (Yang et al.) are both established; the main new element is the two-stage training and pseudo-trajectory supervision scheme, which is somewhat heuristic and not deeply analyzed (e.g., sensitivity to Stage 1 interpolation quality, error propagation from the frozen oracle into Stage 2 supervision).

Evaluation is confined to synthetic/controlled datasets (D-NeRF, NVFI); no real-world dynamic video benchmarks (e.g., DAVIS, Neu3D, iPhone dataset), which weakens claims of practical applicability to complex scenes.

Some results invite scrutiny: the ~10 dB PSNR margins on NVFI over all baselines are unusually large and would benefit from additional analysis or verification; also, only one qualitative figure (single scene) is provided.

Writing/polish issues: a broken cross-reference ('Section ??') in Section 4.1.2, an incorrect figure reference ('shown by 2') in Section 4.3, and the description of 'optional rendering losses' is vague about whether and how they are used in the reported results.

Baselines for extrapolation are relatively few; there is no comparison to simpler alternatives such as extrapolating the deformation MLP via learned velocity/periodic encodings or fitting parametric trajectory models, which would help establish that the full latent-ODE machinery is necessary.
No mention of code release or reproducibility assets; several training details (e.g., trajectory sampling distributions in the sequence separation) are underspecified.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly framed problem: dynamic scene extrapolation is genuinely underexplored compared to interpolation, and the paper articulates why timestamp-conditioned methods fail OOD.

The two-stage decoupling (frozen interpolation model as a trajectory generator, then a Transformer latent ODE forecaster trained on prefix-suffix splits) is a clean and sensible design that aligns with the sequence-to-sequence forecasting literature.

Broad empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (D-NeRF, NVFi, HyperNeRF) with both interpolation-based and extrapolation-oriented baselines, plus a strong ablation suite (ODE formulation, regularization, adaptive scaling, dynamic sampling) including per-scene results.
The ablation against a pure autoregressive Transformer baseline (Table 4) directly supports the central claim that the ODE formulation, not just the architecture, drives the gains.

Additional analyses add depth: deterministic vs. variational formulation comparison, a multi-scene generalization experiment with a held-out scene, and an honest limitations section that identifies failure modes (bouncingballs, trex, fallingball).
Reproducibility is reasonably supported with architecture details, hyperparameters, solver settings, and dataset splits in the appendix.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol has a subtle validity concern: the forecaster is supervised purely by L1 on Gaussian parameters generated by the frozen interpolation model within the observed window, yet extrapolation metrics are computed against real future frames. Reported gains may partly reflect the strength of the underlying interpolation model rather than the ODE forecaster; a stronger attribution analysis (e.g., same forecaster on a weaker interpolation backbone) is missing.

The paper reports remarkably large improvements over GaussianPrediction (up to +10 dB PSNR on Mutant, +7 dB on Standup), but provides no analysis or evidence clarifying whether these gaps come from a fundamentally better forecasting mechanism or from differences in the base 3DGS pipeline; baseline re-implementation details and fairness of comparisons are under-specified.

The model appears to be trained per scene with dataset-specific hyperparameters (e.g., different L_init and temperature per dataset), which limits practicality and weakens claims of generalizable scene dynamics understanding; the multi-scene experiment is only preliminary and confirms per-scene training still wins.

Abstract claims a 19.8% improvement while the contributions claim 21.4%/7.4%/30.5% for individual metrics; the numbers should be consistent. Some per-scene results (e.g., Bouncingballs where Ours trails 4D-GS/Deformable-GS by ~5 dB) are glossed over in the main text.

No computational cost analysis (training time, memory, ODE solver NFEs, inference speed) despite neural ODE integration being notoriously expensive; a runtime comparison with baselines is needed to substantiate practical relevance.
Ablations are only performed on NVFi; ablations on D-NeRF and especially the real-world HyperNeRF dataset would strengthen the evidence, given the large performance gaps reported.
Writing has minor issues (typos such as 'split-banan', 'chickchicken' naming, 'dynamics scenes', inconsistent table formatting between Table 1/2 and Table 3 highlight conventions).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored problem — temporal extrapolation (forecasting) of dynamic 3D scenes rather than interpolation — and clearly articulates why timestamp-conditioned deformation methods fail out-of-distribution beyond the observed window.

The two-stage design (frozen interpolation model as a trajectory generator, then a Transformer latent-ODE forecaster) is cleanly motivated and described; the dynamic prefix–suffix sampling strategy for variable forecasting horizons is a sensible training idea.

Evaluation spans three benchmarks (D-NeRF, NVFi, HyperNeRF) with standard metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS), includes ablations of the ODE formulation, regularization, adaptive weighting, and dynamic sampling, a deterministic-vs-variational comparison, and a preliminary multi-scene generalization study.
The limitations section is candid about failure cases (fast small objects, abrupt dynamics) and correctly identifies that quality is bounded by the upstream interpolation model.
weaknesses: Overclaiming contradicted by the paper's own tables. The text claims ODE-GS 'consistently surpasses' baselines on D-NeRF, yet on Bouncingballs its PSNR (24.91) is well below 4D-GS (29.55) and TiNeuVox (25.92), and on Trex it trails 4D-GS (22.04 vs 23.83). On NVFi fallingball, Ours (22.62) is far below NVFi (31.37) and TiNeuVox (30.00). On HyperNeRF, the method wins only inconsistently (e.g., slice-banana PSNR and keyboard/3dprinter SSIM/LPIPS are second-best at best), yet the abstract and conclusion assert state-of-the-art across all three benchmarks. Aggregate 'improvement percentages' (19.8% in the abstract vs 21.4%/7.4%/30.5% in the intro) are also inconsistent and averaging relative gains across incomparable metrics (PSNR in dB, LPIPS) is statistically dubious.

The core supervision is circular: the forecaster is trained exclusively on trajectories generated by the frozen interpolation model, with suffix 'ground truth' also produced by that same model within the observed window. The model therefore only learns to continue the deformation field's own smooth trajectories and never sees real future dynamics; much of the reported gain likely reflects this smooth-continuation prior rather than genuine learned prediction. This deserves much more critical analysis than it receives.

Limited novelty. The method is a fairly direct combination of known components: latent ODEs (Rubanova et al., 2019), Transformer encoding, canonical-plus-deformation 3DGS (Yang et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2024), and smoothness regularizers. The closest prior, GaussianPrediction, already performs motion-conditioned extrapolation; the delta is mainly replacing discrete GCN prediction with a latent ODE, and the paper does not convincingly argue why this is a fundamental advance over a carefully engineered sequence forecaster.

Per-scene training. The extrapolation model is trained separately for every scene, which substantially limits practical significance for the stated applications (self-driving, robotics). The multi-scene experiment is relegated to the appendix, performs worse than per-scene training (30.72 vs 33.43 average PSNR), and is described only as 'preliminary'.

Ablation evidence is weak and mixed: regularizer and adaptive-weighting ablations only improve the NVFi average by ~0.5 dB, and per-scene results (Table 7) show the regularizers hurt several scenes (e.g., fan 34.96→33.49, bat 37.43→36.68, telescope 36.23→36.57). Ablations are only run on one dataset.

Evaluation protocol clarity is lacking: it is not stated whether baseline numbers are reproduced under the identical train/test temporal splits (e.g., D-NeRF 80/20) or copied from prior papers, and several baseline results (e.g., GaussianPredict at 12.25 PSNR on Lego) look implausibly low, raising concerns about fair comparison. Hyperparameter differences per dataset (Tc, temperatures, loss limits) also suggest significant per-benchmark tuning.

Missing analyses that matter for a forecasting method: performance as a function of extrapolation horizon, sensitivity to ODE solver settings, runtime/cost relative to baselines, and any quantitative measure of 'physical plausibility' beyond smoothness penalties.

Presentation issues: several typos ('slice-banan', 'mult-scene', 'dynamics scenes', 'Where Ibi'), a dangling reference ('as shown in 5'), and claims in the text that do not match table highlights undermine confidence in care of execution.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem—temporal extrapolation (future prediction) of dynamic 3D scenes—as opposed to the interpolation focus of most dynamic NVS work, and the motivation is well articulated.

The two-stage design (freeze an interpolation model, then train a sequence-to-sequence latent-ODE forecaster on generated Gaussian trajectories) is sensible, clearly presented, and the dynamic prefix–suffix sampling strategy is a thoughtful training detail.

Evaluation covers three benchmarks (D-NeRF, NVFi, HyperNeRF) with both synthetic and real scenes, includes the most relevant extrapolation baselines (GaussianPrediction, NVFi), and is supported by ablations (w/o ODE, w/o regularizers, w/o adaptive scaling, w/o dynamic sampling) and qualitative residual maps.

The paper is transparent about limitations (failure on bouncingballs, trex, fallingball; dependence on the interpolation model's quality) and includes useful appendix material, including a deterministic-vs-variational comparison and a multi-scene generalization experiment.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially the standard Latent ODE forecaster (Rubanova et al., 2019) applied to per-Gaussian parameter trajectories, plugged on top of an existing canonical+deformation 3DGS model (Deformable 3D Gaussians). The claimed 'smoothness priors' via regularizers are also fairly standard; the technical contribution is a straightforward composition of known components.

There are internal inconsistencies between the claims and the tables. The text claims 'state of the art across nearly all sequences' on NVFi and 'improving metrics by 19.8%', yet Table 2 shows the method losing substantially on fallingball (22.62 vs. TiNeuVox 30.00 and NVFi 31.37) and Table 1 shows losses on Bouncingballs. Percentage improvements over PSNR ('21.4% PSNR improvement') are a misleading metric since PSNR is logarithmic; absolute dB gains or per-metric reporting would be more honest.

Several baseline numbers look suspiciously rounded or inconsistent (e.g., NVFi and GaussianPredict LPIPS entries in Table 2 reported to exactly two decimals like .0400, .0210), raising questions about how baselines were evaluated—whether the exact same extrapolation protocol, train/test split, and timestamp ranges were used for all methods is not adequately explained.

The extrapolation model is trained per scene on trajectories produced by a frozen per-scene interpolation model, so the forecasting stage largely memorizes a single scene's dynamics; significance and generality are limited, and the multi-scene experiment (Table 8) shows clear degradation when weights are shared. There is also a subtle evaluation circularity risk: the forecaster is supervised on interpolated (model-generated) 'ground-truth' suffixes near the extrapolation boundary rather than on observed images.

Ablations are only averaged over NVFi, and per-scene results (Tables 6–7) show the full method is not uniformly better (e.g., 'w/o regularizers' beats the full model on factory, bat, fan, shark), so the contribution of the proposed regularizers is weaker than claimed.

No computational analysis: ODE integration over 10-dim trajectories per Gaussian at scale is likely expensive; no runtime, memory, or inference-speed comparison is provided, which matters for the advertised robotics/AR applications.

Missing evaluation of longer-horizon behavior (how quality degrades with extrapolation distance), no error bars or repeated runs, and no uncertainty quantification despite the forecasting task being inherently ill-posed—the variational variant is relegated to the appendix with dramatically worse numbers that go largely unexplained.
